phase1.explanation:
Take a breath — Unit 3's the one where your programs stopped assuming everything goes right.

Everything up to this unit trusted the world to cooperate: the file's there, the input's valid, nothing runs out of memory. [[key:Unit 3 was about building programs that survive when that trust turns out to be misplaced]] — exceptions for when logic goes wrong, streams for genuinely getting data in and out of files, and a real defensive-programming mindset underneath all of it.

The exception half: [[term:try-catch-finally]] is the actual catching mechanism, [[term:throw]] creates one exception right now while [[term:throws]] just declares a possibility, and custom exceptions (extends Exception for checked, extends RuntimeException for unchecked) let you invent error types specific to your own program's domain instead of stretching Java's built-in ones to fit.

The I/O half moved through layers, each one wrapping the last: [[term:byte streams]] for raw binary data, [[term:character streams]] for text with real encoding handling, [[term:buffered streams]] wrapping either one to cut down on slow disk trips, and PrintWriter for genuinely convenient formatted output. Then File and its newer, more fail-loud replacement, NIO's Path/Files, both dealing with files as objects rather than just data flowing through them. Serialization let you save a whole object's state to disk and rebuild it later. CSV tied it all together as one very common real-world format built entirely on top of what you'd already learned.

[[warn:the mindset worth carrying forward more than any single class name]]: [[key:assume the file might not be there, the input might be wrong, the disk might be full — and build for that reality instead of hoping around it]]. An empty catch block that just swallows an exception silently is almost always worse than letting the program crash loudly, because at least a crash tells someone something's actually wrong.

Next up: Unit 4, Collections & Threads — organizing data at scale, and doing more than one thing at once.

mcq.question:
Which practice makes a program MORE robust?

A) Using empty catch blocks to ignore all exceptions
B) Checking for null before accessing objects
C) Reading one byte at a time from a large file
D) Not closing files after use
E) Using System.out.println() for all errors

Select the BEST practice.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: the "never leave a catch block empty" advice is old enough to have its own well-known nickname among Java developers — "exception swallowing" — and static analysis tools like SonarQube and even some IDEs flag empty catch blocks as a code smell by default, precisely because they're one of the most common ways real production bugs go undiagnosed for months.
